name: Norwood scale

lead: The Norwood scale (Hamilton-Norwood) grades male pattern hair loss in seven stages, from a full head of hair at stage 1 to a narrow band of hair around the sides and back at stage 7. Placing your hairline on it helps you decide when to start treatment, whether a transplant makes sense, or whether a cropped or buzzed look suits you best.

It builds on James B. Hamilton's 1951 work and a 1975 revision by dermatologist O'Tar Norwood after studying 1,000 patients, which added the A variants for frontal recession. Dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons use it to describe severity and monitor change, and trials use it to define who is included.

paras: People compare photos of their hairline and crown against the chart, track their stage over time, and match treatments or styles to it. Looksmaxxing forums use stage numbers as shared shorthand, from NW0 hairlines to baldmaxxing at later stages.

The scale itself carries no risk. It is a visual classification, and reviewers report variable agreement between raters, limited fit for non-white populations, no information on how fast loss will progress, and a risk of self-misstaging, for example when judging wet hair.

angle.text: Users place their hairline on the seven-stage Norwood chart to size up male pattern hair loss and choose among treatments, transplants, hair systems or a buzz cut. It is the standard clinical classification used by dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons.

lead: The Hamilton-Norwood scale, commonly called the Norwood scale, is a classification of male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) in seven main stages. It is widely used by dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons to describe severity, plan treatment and monitor change over time. [1][2]

The system goes back to James B. Hamilton's 1951 work, which described patterns of male baldness and linked them to androgens. In 1975 dermatologist O'Tar Norwood revised the scheme after studying 1,000 patients, simplifying it to seven stages and adding the 'A' variants. [1][2]

Studies of androgenetic alopecia use the scale to define who is included and to describe severity, including trials of treatments and observational research on associated conditions. [3][4][5] In looksmaxxing forums it also acts as shared vocabulary for hairline status, from 'NW0' hairlines to 'baldmaxxing' at later stages. [2]
infobox: James B. Hamilton (1951); revised by O'Tar Norwood (1975)

paras: Stage 1 is a full head of hair without significant loss. Stage 2 has slight temporal recession, often considered a normal mature hairline. Stage 3 is the first stage generally regarded as clinically significant, with a visible M- or V-shaped frontal recession, and stage 3 vertex adds early crown thinning. [1]

Stage 4 shows further frontal recession and a distinct bald area at the crown separated by a band of hair. In stage 5 the bald areas are larger and the separating band is narrower and sparser, in stage 6 the frontal and crown areas merge leaving a horseshoe fringe, and in stage 7 only a narrow band of hair remains around the sides and back. [1][2]
The 'A' variants (2A to 5A) describe patterns in which hair recedes uniformly from the front without a separate crown patch. [1]

James B. Hamilton introduced a systematic grading of male pattern hair loss in 1951, describing distinct patterns and linking the process to androgens. His eight-type system was considered complex to apply visually. [1][2]

O'Tar Norwood, a dermatologist who began performing hair transplants in 1961, published 'Male Pattern Baldness: Classification and Incidence' in the Southern Medical Journal in 1975 after studying 1,000 white men. Norwood later helped found the International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery in 1993, and by the 1990s the combined system was the most widely used classification. [2]

Clinicians use the scale with history, scalp examination, photography and trichoscopy to stage hair loss, track progression and check treatment response. [2] Reviews of androgenetic alopecia describe it as the scale used to classify male pattern hair loss, with the Ludwig scale preferred for women. [4]

Researchers use it to define study populations. A scoping review of early-onset androgenetic alopecia reported that the Hamilton-Norwood scale was the most common tool for grading in the studies it covered. [5] Trials of minoxidil adjuvants and botulinum toxin have enrolled men by stage, for example stages 2 to 6 or III to V. [3][6]

A study in the International Journal of Trichology examined the reliability of the Hamilton-Norwood classification. [7] Grokipedia's summary says agreement between raters varies, with some studies describing dermatologists' agreement as unsatisfactory and others reporting kappa values of about 0.6 to 0.8, and Wikipedia states inter-examiner reliability is only moderate. [1][2]

Reviewers also note that the scale was built largely on Caucasian men, is purely visual, does not predict the speed of progression, and can be misapplied through self-assessment, such as evaluating wet hair. [1][2]

Studies using the scale have examined links between early-onset androgenetic alopecia and metabolic features. An Indian cross-sectional study of 100 men under 30 with grade 3 or higher loss reported altered hormonal profiles in 34 and insulin resistance in 44, with altered hormones associated with more severe loss. [8] Other case-control studies in Singapore, Turkey and India have examined insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome in early androgenetic alopecia. [9][10][11]

An observational study of 300 hospitalized COVID-19 patients reported more frequent and severe androgenetic alopecia among men with worse outcomes. [12] A Canadian case-control study examined vertex baldness and prostate cancer odds, while a separate study concluded that androgenic alopecia is not useful as an indicator of high prostate cancer risk. [13][14]

A 2022 randomized, blinded placebo-controlled trial enrolled 24 men with androgenetic alopecia (Norwood average 4.4, range 2 to 6) and reported that 75 percent of those who used a SULT1A1 adjuvant with topical minoxidil regrew hair over 60 days versus 33 percent with a sham adjuvant. [3] A 2025 randomized trial of 15 men at Hamilton-Norwood stages III to V compared two ways of giving botulinum toxin A for androgenetic alopecia. [6]

A review of platelet-rich plasma in androgenetic alopecia notes that the Hamilton-Norwood scale is used to assess severity and that by age 60 about 45 percent of men and 35 percent of women develop the condition. [4] No trials have tested the scale itself as an intervention. These studies use the scale to describe participants.

Grokipedia reports that online communities such as 'baldmaxxers' present stage 7 as a deliberate, confident look and that historical attitudes to baldness range from dignity to disfigurement. [2] Psychological research summarized there links androgenetic alopecia to lower self-esteem and distress. [2]

timeline.event: James B. Hamilton publishes a systematic grading of male pattern hair loss. [1][2]
O'Tar Norwood revises the system after studying 1,000 patients, creating the seven-stage scale with 'A' variants. [1][2]
Norwood helps found the International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery. [2]
A reliability study of the Hamilton-Norwood classification is published. [2][7]
